title: Cast Iron Green Beans with Ham Hock & Potatoes
wood: None — Dutch oven on the stove or over coals
finish: Beans silky, potatoes poke-tender, vinegar in at the end
summary: Ham hock pot liquor, whole potatoes, snapped beans. Vinegar last. Taste before you salt.
story: This is pot liquor cooking, not a crisp skillet sauté. The hock simmers first so the broth tastes like smoke and bone before the beans ever hit the pot. Fresh beans go in raw and come out silky. Canned beans wait until the last 20–30 minutes or they fall apart. Country ham is saltier than a hock — cut the bouillon and don't salt until you've tasted.

items: 2 lbs fresh green beans, ends snapped (or 4 cans, drained — see notes)
1 large smoked ham hock, 1–1.5 lbs (or a ½–¾ lb chunk of country ham)
1½ lbs small whole potatoes, scrubbed, skins on
4 cups chicken broth (or 4 cups water + 4 tsp chicken bouillon)
1 Tbsp apple cider vinegar, stirred in at the end

steps.body: Ham hock (or country ham) and broth in the Dutch oven, lid on. Gentle simmer 45–60 minutes.
steps.title: Build the pot liquor

steps.body: Lift the meat out. Add onions, potatoes, and fresh green beans. Nestle the meat back on top. Broth should nearly cover; splash in water if short.
steps.title: Load the pot

steps.body: Lid on, low simmer 45 minutes to an hour, until beans are silky and potatoes poke tender.
steps.title: Simmer low

steps.body: Fish out the meat, chop it, stir it back in.
steps.title: Chop the meat back in

steps.body: Stir in the vinegar, then taste before salting.
steps.title: Vinegar, then taste

proTips.text: It's saltier than a hock — cut the bouillon in half (or use low-sodium broth) and don't add any salt until you've tasted at the end.
They're already cooked. Don't put them in with the potatoes or they'll fall apart. Add the drained cans for just the last 20–30 minutes so they soak up flavor without going mushy.

milestones.hint: Meat chopped back in. Taste before salt.
milestones.label: Vinegar in

title: Pit-Smoked Zesty Mac & Cheese
wood: Hickory, oak, or pecan — not mesquite
summary: Three-cheese sauce, jalapeño heat, panko crust. Smoke it just long enough to kiss it, not bury it.
story: Cheese takes smoke fast. This one lives in a 9x13 or a cast-iron skillet on the pit at 250–275°F with mild wood. Shred your own cheese or the sauce goes grainy. Season a notch louder than you want — the smoke will calm it down.

items: 1 lb elbow macaroni or cavatappi, cooked 2 minutes shy of package time, drained
1 tsp hot sauce, plus more to taste
2–3 jalapeños, diced (leave some seeds for more fire)
Salt and black pepper to taste
1 tsp BBQ rub (or paprika + pinch of cayenne)
½ lb bacon, cooked crisp and crumbled, folded in

steps.title: Fire and pasta
steps.body: Pit at 250–275°F. Mild wood — hickory, oak, or pecan. Not mesquite. Cook pasta 2 minutes shy of done. Drain.

steps.title: Roux, then dairy
steps.body: Melt butter, whisk in flour, cook 1 minute. Whisk in evaporated milk and cream. Simmer until it coats a spoon.

steps.title: Cheese off the heat
steps.body: Melt in cream cheese, then shredded cheeses a handful at a time. Stir in mustard, onion and garlic powder, hot sauce, and jalapeños. Season bolder than you want — smoke mellows it.

steps.title: Pan and crust
steps.body: Fold in pasta. Spread in a greased 9x13 foil pan or cast iron. Toss panko with melted butter and rub; scatter over the top.

steps.title: Smoke, then rest
steps.body: Uncovered on the pit 45–60 minutes until bubbly and golden. Rest 10 minutes so it sets. If it looks dry coming off, stir in a splash of warm cream.

proTips.text: Shred your own cheese. Bagged shreds have starch that turns the sauce grainy.
Don't oversmoke it. Cheese picks up smoke fast — an hour is plenty.

milestones.label: Sauce coats a spoon
milestones.hint: Then pull off heat and melt cheese.

title: Smoked Christmas Ham
summary: Fully cooked bone-in ham, pineapple rings, cherries, and a brown-sugar pineapple glaze. Mild fruit wood. Don't blast it.
story: The ham already took a smoke once at the plant. What you are doing is warming it through and laying on a sticky glaze so the table looks like Christmas. Pin pineapple rings with a cherry in the middle, hold 250°F, and stop at 140°F. Hotter and the sugar scorches; past 145°F and it dries out. The drippings in the foil pan are liquid gold — spoon them over the slices.

items: 1 (8–10 lb) fully cooked bone-in ham (spiral-sliced or shank portion)
1 can pineapple rings in juice (reserve the juice)
¼ cup pineapple juice (from the can)
2 Tbsp Dijon mustard (or yellow for milder)

steps.body: Apple or cherry wood — mild fruit smoke suits ham best. It's already smoked once, so don't blast it. Hold 250°F; hotter and the sugar glaze can scorch.
steps.title: Pit at 250°F

steps.body: If the ham is not spiral-sliced, score the fat in a diamond pattern so the glaze sinks in.
steps.title: Score if you need to

steps.body: Pin pineapple rings all over the ham with toothpicks, a cherry in the center of each ring.
steps.title: Pineapple and cherries

steps.body: Set the ham in a foil pan (catches the drippings for basting) and brush on a first coat of glaze.
steps.title: First glaze

steps.body: Smoke 2.5–3.5 hours, brushing with glaze every 30–45 minutes, until the inside reads 140°F.
steps.title: Smoke and mop

steps.body: Last 30 minutes: lay on a final thick coat of glaze and let it tack up.
steps.title: Final coat

steps.body: Rest 15 minutes tented with foil before carving. Spoon the pan drippings over the slices.
steps.title: Rest and carve

proTips.text: Don't push past 140–145°F internal or it dries out. This is a warm-through, not a cook.
Hold 250°F. The sugar will scorch if you chase heat.
325°F, about 15 minutes per pound, same glaze schedule.

milestones.hint: 250°F, apple or cherry, ham in a foil pan.
milestones.label: On the pit

milestones.hint: Final thick coat, let it tack. Rest 15 minutes.
milestones.label: 140°F

title: Honey-Glazed Smoked Turkey Breast
summary: HoneyBaked-style bone-in turkey breast. Overnight brine, maple smoke at 275–300°F, honey-brown sugar glaze until it crackles.
story: This is the HoneyBaked copy without the spiral slicer. Brine overnight so the breast stays wet through a 275–300°F smoke. Maple is mild and a little sweet — made for poultry. Glaze starts around 145–150°F and gets a fresh coat every 15 minutes. Pull at 160°F. Carryover finishes it at a safe 165°F. Stir extra sugar into the last coat if you want that candy-shell crackle.

items: 2 Tbsp olive oil or melted butter
1 tsp kosher salt if brined (1 Tbsp if not)

steps.body: Stir salt and brown sugar into a gallon of cold water until dissolved. Submerge the breast and refrigerate 8–12 hours. No fridge room? Inject melted butter whisked with chicken broth throughout the meat instead.
steps.title: Brine overnight

steps.body: Rinse the brine off and pat the breast VERY dry. Rub with oil, then season all over. Optional: work some seasoned butter under the skin.
steps.title: Dry and season

steps.body: Pit at 275–300°F with maple wood splits. Mild and slightly sweet, made for poultry. Don't smoke poultry below 275°F — it needs to move through the danger zone.
steps.title: Smoke on maple

steps.body: Smoke until the thickest part hits 145–150°F (about 2–2.5 hours). Brush on the honey glaze, then re-glaze every 15 minutes.
steps.title: Start the glaze

steps.body: Pull at 160°F internal — carryover takes it to a safe 165°F. Rest 20–30 minutes tented with foil before slicing. For extra HoneyBaked-style crackle, stir 2 Tbsp sugar into the final glaze coat.
steps.title: Pull and rest

proTips.text: Don't smoke poultry below 275°F. Low-and-slow is for pork and brisket, not turkey.
Stir 2 Tbsp extra sugar into the last glaze coat and let it tack. That's the candy shell.
Skip the bucket. Inject a stick of melted butter whisked with ½ cup broth.

title: Ember Finishing Glaze
servings: ~1¼ cups — racks or a pulled butt
pitTemp: Warm only — do not reduce it into candy
finish: Thin, pourable, sets tacky — meat still shows through
summary: Sweet-tangy finishing glaze for ribs or pork butt. Thin coat. The pork has to shine, not the bottle.
story: A glaze is a last coat, not a sauce bath. Vinegar and mustard cut the molasses so it doesn’t read candy. Honey gives shine. Worcestershire keeps it savory. Warm it until it loosens — it should coat a spoon and still run. On ribs, one thin pass in the last 15–20 minutes so it sets tacky. On a pork butt, toss the pull while the meat is hot and stop when you can still see bark. Extra in a bowl. If you can’t taste smoke through it, you used too much.

steps.title: Warm until it runs
steps.body: Stir over low heat just until the sugar dissolves and the glaze loosens. Do not boil it down. If it sits in a sheet, thin with vinegar or juice.

steps.title: Ribs — late and thin
steps.body: Last 15–20 minutes on the pit. One thin coat. Lid shut so it sets tacky, not wet. A second kiss only if the first soaked in.

steps.title: Pork butt — after the pull
steps.body: Toss the hot pulled pork with a light coat. Bark should still show. Pass the rest in a bowl.

proTips.text: Sauce is a finishing coat. If you need a soup of it to make the ribs taste like something, the rub and fire didn’t do their job.
Sugar late. Early glaze scorches. Late glaze shines.
If you can’t taste the smoke through it, wipe some off and serve the rest on the side.

milestones.label: Warmed thin
milestones.hint: Coats a spoon and still runs.

milestones.label: Thin coat
milestones.hint: Ribs last 15–20 min, or tossed on hot pulled pork.

title: Apple-Peach Pork Injection
servings: ~3½ cups — enough for an 8–10 lb butt
pitTemp: Warm the liquid only — do not boil
finish: Sugar and salt dissolved, cooled, strained
summary: Apple juice plus peach nectar for pork butt. Enough tang that the fruit doesn’t read candy-sweet.
story: Apple juice is the classic pork-injection base. Peach nectar on top of it makes the mix read Southern instead of just sweet. The vinegar does quiet work — just enough bite to keep all that fruit and sugar from going candy. Warm it so the salt and brown sugar disappear, cool it, strain it, then grid the butt. Rest in the fridge a couple hours or overnight, then rub and smoke as usual. Pork butt is forgiving. Don’t overthink the pattern.

steps.title: Warm and dissolve
steps.body: Warm the mix gently and stir until the sugar and salt disappear. Do not boil — you want it dissolved, not cooked down.

steps.title: Cool and strain
steps.body: Cool to room temp. Strain so powder clumps and any pulp don’t clog the needle.

steps.title: Grid the butt
steps.body: Inject in a 1-inch grid all over. Pork butt is forgiving — don’t overthink the pattern. Some leakage is normal; wipe it and keep going.

steps.title: Rest, then rub
steps.body: Fridge a couple hours or overnight. Then rub and smoke as usual.

proTips.text: The vinegar is doing quiet work here — just enough tang to keep all that fruit and sugar from going candy-sweet.
Peach reads more Southern than straight apple juice ever will. Kern's or any canned nectar is fine.
Strain. A clogged injector mid-butt is how you make a mess and skip half the meat.

milestones.label: Dissolved
milestones.hint: Warm, stir, sugar and salt gone.

milestones.label: Cooled and strained
milestones.hint: Room temp. Fine mesh so the needle stays clear.

milestones.label: Injected
milestones.hint: 1-inch grid. Rest in the fridge, then rub.

title: Ember Brisket Injection
servings: ~2 cups — one packer, heavy on the flat
pitTemp: Warm the liquid only — do not boil
summary: Reduced beef, a shot of coffee, and quiet umami. For a packer — especially the lean flat. Not a phosphate crutch.
story: This is brisket injection. The flat is where it earns its keep. Reduced bone broth, a little coffee, Worcestershire, and a drop of fish sauce. You will not taste coffee or fish. You will taste deeper beef. Season the inside of the lean. Go light on the point — that side already has fat. A clean fire and a real rest still have to do the work. Then salt, pepper, and the same post-oak cook you were going to run anyway.

items: 1½ cups unsalted beef bone broth, reduced by about a third (or 1½ cups water + 1½ Tbsp roasted beef base)
¼ cup strong black coffee, cooled
1 tsp fish sauce (Red Boat or similar — you will not taste fish)
½ tsp kosher salt (skip or cut if the base is already salty)
1 Tbsp melted beef tallow, optional — strain well

steps.title: Warm and dissolve
steps.body: Warm just enough to dissolve the powders and melt the tallow if you are using it. Do not boil.

steps.title: Cool and strain
steps.body: Cool to room temp. Fine-mesh strain. Tallow and coffee fines clog needles. Mix fresh — don’t park overnight with the fat in it.

steps.title: Inject the flat
steps.body: 1-inch grid through the brisket flat. Lighter pass on the point. Leakage is normal. Wipe and keep going.

steps.title: Rest, then rub
steps.body: Fridge 2–12 hours. Then salt and pepper and the same fire you already trust.

proTips.text: This is flavor for the flat, not a crutch. If the fire is dirty and the rest is short, no syringe saves lean brisket.
Coffee is roast. Fish sauce is quiet MSG. Neither should announce itself. If you can name them in the slice, you used too much.
Strain twice if you use tallow. A clogged injector is how you season three spots and skip the rest of the flat.

Don't save this one for brisket. Venison is the leanest meat you'll put on the pit — a backstrap or a hindquarter roast will dry out on you fast. Hit it with this injection first and it stays juicy all the way through the cook.

milestones.label: Flat injected
milestones.hint: 1-inch grid on the lean. Light on the point. Rest, then rub.

title: Holiday Smoked Ham
finish: 135–140°F internal — already cooked, don’t roast it dry
summary: City ham on the pit with a clove-cinnamon glaze. Warm it, smoke it, glaze late. Not a 12-hour hostage.
story: A grocery city ham is already cured and cooked. The job is gentle smoke and a holiday glaze, not another all-day cook. Score the fat, stud a few cloves, run apple or pecan at 250–275°F until the center is 135–140°F. Then the glaze: brown sugar, cider, Dijon, honey, cinnamon, and just enough clove. Two thin coats in the last 20–30 minutes. Rest 20 minutes. Clove and cinnamon should be a hello, not a Yankee Candle.

items: 1 city ham, 10–12 lb, spiral or bone-in
8–12 whole cloves for studding — not a full coat
⅓ cup apple cider or pineapple juice
¼ tsp ground cloves (or 4 whole cloves, fished out after warming)

steps.title: Score and stud
steps.body: Pat the ham dry. Score the fat in diamonds — into the fat, not the meat. Stud a few cloves in the diamonds. A handful. Not the whole ham.

steps.title: Warm with clean smoke
steps.body: 250–275°F, apple or pecan, cut-side down. A 10–12 lb ham is often 2½–3½ hours. Start probing at 2 hours. Target 135–140°F. It is already cooked.

steps.title: Warm the glaze
steps.body: Stir the glaze over low heat until the sugar dissolves. Thin enough to brush. Fish out whole cloves if you used them.

steps.title: Two thin coats
steps.body: Last 20–30 minutes. Brush one coat. Let it set. Brush a second. Pull at 140°F. Rest 20 minutes before slicing.

proTips.text: Past 145°F a city ham starts giving the water back. Warm it. Don’t cook it twice.
If it smells like potpourri you used too much clove. A quarter teaspoon ground is plenty for a cup of glaze.
Cold slices, biscuits, or fried ham with eggs. Don’t microwave a spiral — it weeps.

title: Pitt Style Amber Ham
finish: 145–155°F after the amber sauce — thin, not candy
summary: Pittsburgh ham barbecue with smoke first. Thin sweet-tangy red sauce that cooks down amber. Chipped onto a toasted kaiser.
story: In the Burgh this is not pulled pork. It is chipped ham in a ketchup-vinegar-brown-sugar sauce piled on a kaiser. Ember smokes a bone-in ham first so you get bark, then finishes it in that same thin red sauce until it turns amber and sticky. Same sandwich. Better fire. The sauce stays thin — it soaks the meat; it is not Kansas City paste.

items: 1 bone-in smoked ham, 7–10 lb (or 1½–3 lb chipped chopped ham for the fast version)
Yellow mustard or oil as binder
Ember House Rub, or brown sugar, paprika, black pepper, garlic, pinch of cinnamon
½ small onion, minced (or 1 tsp onion powder)
Optional: ½ cup amber ale, splash of pickle juice, pinch of cayenne
Kaiser rolls or soft hamburger buns, toasted

steps.title: Rub the ham
steps.body: Pat dry. Light binder, then rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250°F over apple or cherry until about 130–140°F internal. Spritz with apple juice if the surface dries.

steps.title: Make the amber sauce
steps.body: Melt butter, sweat the onion, add ketchup, water, vinegar, brown sugar, Worcestershire, mustard. Simmer 10 minutes until it thins and turns amber-red. Ale at the end if you use it.

steps.title: Finish in the sauce
steps.body: Move the ham to a pan. Pour sauce over and around. Cover loosely. Continue at 250–275°F until 145–155°F and the glaze is lacquered.

steps.title: Chip and pile
steps.body: Rest 20–30 minutes. Slice thin or chip it. Toss in the pan sauce. Pile on toasted rolls. Relish on top. Fast version: skip the smoke, simmer sauce 10 minutes, stir in chipped ham, heat 5–7 minutes.

proTips.text: The sauce should stay thin. If it sits like molasses you cooked it too long.
Thick-sliced ham is the wrong texture. Chip it until it looks like confetti.
No smoker? The skillet version is the original lunch-counter sandwich. Don’t skip the toasted roll.

milestones.label: Amber sauce
milestones.hint: Thin, red going amber. Ten-minute simmer.

milestones.label: Glazed and chipped
milestones.hint: 145–155°F. Thin slices. Relish on the roll.

title: Bacon-Wrapped Venison Tenderloin Bites
summary: The first thing gone at every deer camp. Tenderloin medallions wrapped in bacon, kissed with smoke, finished with Ember Finishing Glaze.
story: These don't make it to the table half the time. Thin bacon, a sweet-heat rub, and a hot enough pit to render the fat before the venison sees 140. That's the whole trick — everything else is just getting out of the way.

items: 1 1/2 to 2 lb venison tenderloin, silverskin removed
12 slices thin-cut bacon, cut in half

steps.title: Cut medallions
steps.body: Cut the tenderloin into 1 1/2-inch medallions, all roughly the same thickness so they cook even.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Mix the rub and coat every medallion on all sides.

steps.title: Wrap
steps.body: Wrap each medallion with a half-slice of bacon and pin with a soaked toothpick. Snug, not strangled.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 275°F for 45 to 60 minutes, until the bacon renders and starts to crisp and the venison reads 130-135°F inside.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Brush on the Ember Finishing Glaze during the last 10 minutes so it tacks up instead of burning.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes, pull the toothpicks, and serve warm.

proTips.text: Thin bacon beats thick here. Thick bacon won't render before the tenderloin overcooks.
Past 140°F these dry out fast. Pull at 130 and let carryover do the rest.
Make a double batch. You'll thank yourself.

title: Smoked Venison Jerky
summary: Real smoked jerky — chewy, peppery, with actual smoke on it. The cure keeps it safe, the low smoke keeps it tender.
story: Store jerky is a rumor of meat. This is the real thing — venison sliced thin, cured right, and smoked low until it bends and cracks. A splash of pineapple juice in the marinade adds a sweet-tangy note, but mind the clock: those enzymes work fast. Takes a day of waiting and an afternoon of watching, and you'll never buy a bag again.

items: 3 lb venison roast (eye of round or hindquarter), all fat and silverskin trimmed
1/2 tsp Prague Powder #1 (pink curing salt) — do not skip
1 tsp red pepper flakes (optional, for heat)

steps.title: Slice
steps.body: Partially freeze the roast 1 to 2 hours until firm. Slice 1/4-inch thick against the grain.

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk everything else into the marinade and coat the slices completely in a zip bag or covered pan.

steps.title: Wait
steps.body: Refrigerate 8 to 12 hours, turning once. The pineapple's enzymes work fast — don't push past 12 hours or the meat goes mushy.

steps.title: Rack up
steps.body: Lay the slices on oiled smoker grates with space between them. Pat lightly — tacky, not dripping.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 170-180°F for 4 to 6 hours. Start checking at 4: it's done when a cooled piece bends and cracks but doesn't break, and reads 160°F inside.

steps.title: Store
steps.body: Cool completely, then bag it. Refrigerate for long keeping — it'll last weeks in the fridge, if it survives the week.

proTips.text: The cure is food safety, not optional. It keeps the low-temp smoke safe.
Uniform slices = uniform jerky. The freezer trick is the whole secret.
Judge doneness on a cooled piece — hot jerky always feels softer than it is.

milestones.label: Done
milestones.hint: Bends and cracks. Cool, bag, refrigerate.

title: Smoked Leg of Lamb with Garlic, Rosemary, and Pesto
summary: Lamb on the smoker is a sleeper hit. Garlic and rosemary pressed into a scored fat cap, gentle smoke, pulled pink, finished with fresh pesto.
story: The people who say they don't like lamb just never had it like this. Score the fat cap, work the garlic-rosemary paste in deep, let the smoke do the rest — then spoon fresh pesto over the slices so it stays bright.

items: 1 bone-in leg of lamb, 5 to 7 lb
3 Tbsp fresh rosemary, chopped (or 1 Tbsp dried)
1 cup basil pesto, for spooning over the slices

steps.title: Trim and score
steps.body: Trim the leg of surface silver and excess fat, leaving a 1/4-inch fat cap. Score the cap in a diamond pattern so the rub gets in.

steps.title: Paste
steps.body: Mash the olive oil, garlic, rosemary, salt, pepper, Dijon, and lemon juice into a paste. Rub it all over the leg, working it into the scores. Rest at room temp 45 minutes while the pit heats.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250°F until the thickest part reads 130-135°F, about 3 to 4 hours depending on size.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 20 to 30 minutes tented in foil — the temp will climb a few degrees.

steps.title: Slice and finish
steps.body: Slice against the grain and serve, with the pesto spooned over the top. Save the bone — it makes a hell of a pot of beans.

proTips.text: Lamb wants medium-rare. Past 145°F it tightens up and dries out fast.
Bone-in cooks more evenly and stays juicier than boneless.
Cherry wood gives the crust a beautiful color; oak keeps the smoke in the background.

milestones.label: Served
milestones.hint: Rested, sliced, pesto over the top.
